Metabolism of Dietary Nucleic Acids in Humans
The human diet is naturally rich in nucleic acids because food is derived from once-living organisms. Because, as already described,
nucleotides and nucleosides can be synthesized de novo and nucleobases liberated during catabolism can be salvaged, they are often
considered to be dispensable nutrients in food. The metabolism of these exogenous nucleic acids follows a similar pattern to the
intracellular process described above, but the bacterial ﬂora of the intestine are the ﬁrst point of degradation. This digestion is rapid.
Studies in both pigs and humans demonstrated that up to 50% of dietary purine was degraded to carbon dioxide within 30 min,
43% was recovered in the urine and 5% excreted in the feces. Less than 2% of dietary purines is incorporated into nucleic acids.
Humans thus have no apparent essential requirement for purines from the diet and the intestinal mucosa provides an effective
barrier to their uptake through a battery of enzymes that can rapidly degrade purine nucleotides, nucleosides, and bases especially
unusual purines found in plant materials. Because of this enzyme activity, and the rapid turnover of intestinal mucosa, approxi-
